screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we'll follow how raw posts become a personalized news feed. You'll learn the two common aggregation patterns — push and pull — why merging many sources can become a bottleneck, and how ranking transforms thousands of candidate posts into a compact, relevant set. We'll examine the signals used by modern ranking: recency, engagement, relationship strength, content type and author authority. Think of this chapter as the roadmap that connects storage and fanout choices to the user-facing ordering that drives engagement. How would you balance recency and engagement for your product? That question will guide much of our examples.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.4 › News Feed — Overview

News Feed — Feed Generation & Ranking

How we collect candidate posts, score them, and deliver a compact, personalized timeline that balances freshness and engagement.

In this lesson
Aggregation patterns, ranking signals, scoring, ML, and production considerations.
Why it matters
Ordering drives engagement; the right ranker surfaces content users want.
What you'll build
A simple ranking heuristic and a mental model for production trade-offs.
Quick Map
  • Aggregation: Collect candidates from followed users or precomputed inboxes.
  • Merging: Use heaps to combine sorted lists and find top-K efficiently.
  • Ranking: Score candidates by recency, engagement, relationship, and ML features.
Operational beats
  • Real-time freshness via push or WebSocket notifications.
  • Cache ranked segments to avoid repeated heavy computation.
  • A/B test ranking weights and ML models continuously.
Explore Key Topics
Feed aggregation, ranking heuristics vs learned models, operational trade-offs that keep feeds fast and fresh.
Visual Concept
Raw posts
Multiple authors generate posts stored in user post lists or a global posts table.
Aggregation
Pulls or precomputed inboxes supply candidate posts to the Feed Service.
Ranking
A scoring function or ML model orders candidates for presentation.
Starting point
Decide whether to precompute (push) or compute on-request (pull). That choice shapes latency, storage and complexity.

You will name the principal signals used to rank posts — recency, engagement, relationship strength, content type and author credibility — and you will be able to write a simple weighted scoring function combining these signals. Finally, you'll be able to discuss production concerns: real-time freshness strategies, the cold-start problem for new users, the risk of filter bubbles, and practical mitigations like caching and A/B testing. Each objective combines definition with practice: you will see concrete examples and a small Python heuristic to implement and test locally. These competencies prepare you to design feed subsystems that balance latency, accuracy, and compute cost.

keyIdea.title: Practice focus
keyIdea.text: Balance theory with measurements: implement a heuristic, measure impact, and iterate with A/B tests and caching to manage cost.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.4 › Practice & Trade-offs
Experiment Goals
  • Implement: A weighted scoring heuristic.
  • Measure: Ranking order changes, CTR and latency.
  • Iterate: Adjust weights, cache layers, precompute rules.
When to be conservative

If ranking changes impact retention, favor slower rollouts and small A/B increments. Avoid over-personalization early in a product's lifecycle.

Example scenario

A user follows 1,000 accounts. Fetching 10 posts per account yields 10,000 candidates. Without efficient merging and scoring, that request is expensive. A heap-based top-K or precomputed inbox reduces the work dramatically.

screens.title: Push vs Pull vs Hybrid Aggregation
screens.narratorSegment: Aggregation is the stage where candidate posts are gathered before ranking. In a push-based system, when an author publishes a post the system fans out that post to the followers' inboxes — those per-user stores already contain the candidates, so a feed request simply reads a small pre-ordered list. This minimizes read-time latency but increases write amplification and storage. In a pull-based system the feed service identifies whom the user follows and fetches recent posts from each followed account when the user requests a feed. Pull reduces write cost and storage, but it can produce large candidate sets and higher read latency. A hybrid approach precomputes popular authors' posts while pulling for less active accounts, balancing cost and latency. Consider a user who follows a thousand accounts: a pure pull that fetches ten posts per account creates ten thousand candidates; that is the classic merging problem. The practical rule is to push when reads vastly outnumber writes and storage is acceptable, pull when writes dominate or storage is constrained, and hybrid when neither extreme fits. A misconception is to assume push is always better — it can cause excessive storage and updating for high-write users. Question: given your product's read/write profile, which strategy will likely give better user-perceived latency?

keyIdea.title: Aggregation trade-off
keyIdea.text: Push reduces read latency by precomputing, pull reduces write and storage cost. Hybrid mixes both to balance load.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.4 › Feed Aggregation
Push-based

Authors' posts are fanned out into followers' inboxes at write time. Feed reads are simple retrievals of a pre-selected list, typically ordered by timestamp.

  • Pros: Low read latency, predictable reads.
  • Cons: High write amplification and storage per follower.
Pull-based

At request time, the service fetches recent posts from each followed account and merges them into candidates. This saves storage but can produce large candidate sets.

  • Pros: Lower write cost and storage.
  • Cons: Higher read-time computation and latency.
Hybrid

Precompute feeds for heavy or popular authors, pull for long-tail accounts. This reduces overall cost while keeping latency reasonable for most users.

Use-case
Combine push for celebrities and pull for casual users.
Concrete example

If a user follows 1,000 accounts and we fetch 10 posts per account, we must merge 10,000 posts. Heap-based top-K or precomputed inboxes are the right mitigations. Always measure your read/write patterns before choosing a strategy.

Key Takeaway

Choose push to speed reads, pull to reduce writes. Hybrid lets you selectively precompute where it matters.

screens.title: Merging Candidate Lists with Heaps
screens.narratorSegment: When a pull or hybrid strategy yields many candidate lists, naive concatenation and sorting is expensive. An efficient approach uses a heap to merge sorted lists and keep only the top-K results. The idea is simple: treat the latest post from each followed user's list as an entry, insert those entries into a min-heap or max-heap sized to K, and then repeatedly pull the next most recent item from the list that produced the popped heap element. This way you never materialize all candidates at once. For example, if you want the top 50 posts from 1,000 followees, you initialize the heap with the newest post from each followee and only fetch the next post from a followee when its head was part of the top-K candidate set. This reduces memory and network reads. Common misconceptions include assuming heaps eliminate all work — they reduce memory and sorting costs but you still need to fetch posts and metadata. Another important point: pick the right heap orientation (min vs max) and choose K that matches the UI (page size plus a small buffer). Practical tip: combine heap merging with caching of recent per-user post lists so the fetchs used by the heap are low-latency. How could you instrument your system to measure savings from heap-based merging?

keyIdea.title: Merging pattern
keyIdea.text: Use a heap to merge sorted per-user lists and compute top-K without loading every candidate into memory.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.4 › Heap-based Merging
Algorithm summary
  1. Initialize heap with newest post from each followee.
  2. Pop the top element into result set.
  3. Push the next post from the same followee into the heap.
  4. Repeat until you have K results.
When this helps
  • Large numbers of followees producing small sorted lists.
  • Desire to avoid full sort of tens of thousands of candidates.
  • When you can fetch per-user lists lazily and cache them.
Concrete example

Top-50 from 1,000 followees: initialize heap with 1,000 newest posts, pop into result and only fetch subsequent posts for followees whose posts were selected. You avoid sorting the full 10,000 candidate set.

Key Takeaway

Heap merging finds top-K efficiently by lazily pulling from sorted sources rather than materializing and sorting all candidates.

screens.title: Ranking Factors — What matters when ordering posts
screens.narratorSegment: Ranking is where the candidate list becomes the user's actual feed. Ranking factors are the measurable features that indicate a post's likely value to a user. Recency remains an important baseline: newer posts are often more relevant. Engagement — likes, comments, shares and views — signals popularity and often correlates with user interest. Relationship strength captures how closely a user interacts with an author, and content type lets you prefer media formats users like. Author authority or credibility acts as a tie-breaker for expert content. Finally, diversity is a design signal used to prevent a feed from being dominated by one source or topic. A simple misconception is treating engagement as absolute truth; high engagement can be misleading due to bots or viral noise, which is why signals are combined and sometimes capped. Another common mistake is over-weighting explicit user preferences, which can create a filter bubble. In practice, a scoring function sums weighted signals and then sorts posts by score. You can test different weight combinations with small experiments to see how ordering and engagement change. Ask yourself: which signal would you reduce to increase serendipity in the feed?

keyIdea.title: Signal mix
keyIdea.text: Combine multiple signals — recency, engagement, relationship, type, authority — and tune weights to balance relevance and diversity.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.4 › Ranking Signals
Recency

Newer posts usually score higher. Recency often uses a decay function so older content gradually loses weight.

Engagement

Likes, comments and shares signal interest. Use caps or transform metrics to avoid runaway popularity bias.

Relationship strength

Prior interactions indicate closeness; prioritize content from frequently interacting authors.

Content type

Prefer formats a user likes, such as video over text, if that aligns with their behavior.

Author authority

Verified or expert authors may get higher weight for credibility-sensitive products.

Diversity

Inject serendipity to avoid echo chambers; occasionally down-weight top authors or topics.

Key Takeaway

Ranking uses many signals. Tune weights carefully and guard against bias and filter bubbles.

screens.title: Scoring Function — A simple weighted example
screens.narratorSegment: A scoring function turns multiple signals into a single numeric priority. A simple form is a weighted sum: Score = W1 * Recency + W2 * Engagement + W3 * Relationship + …. This makes reasoning straightforward: increase a weight to favor a signal, decrease it to reduce influence. The chapter provides a small Python example where recency decays over seven days, engagement aggregates likes and comments with different weights, and relationship strength is an external feature. In practice, you should cap extreme values, normalize different signals, and consider transforms like logarithms for counts. A common misconception is to assume more signals always improve quality — noisy or correlated signals can add instability. Another is to place absolute trust in the initial weights; A/B testing and logging are essential to validate that your weight choices lift metrics. Concrete example: weight recency at 0.5, engagement at 0.3 and relationship at 0.2 and observe how a very recent low-engagement post might outrank an older high-engagement post. The final question is: what tradeoff do you accept between freshness and popularity for your feed?

keyIdea.text: A weighted sum is interpretable and easy to try; normalize and cap signals and validate weights with experiments.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.4 › Scoring Function
Formula (schematic)

Score = W1 * Recency_Score + W2 * Engagement_Score + W3 * Relationship_Score + ...

Normalize each component, cap extremes and use transforms (log) for raw counts.

Concrete scenario

If you weight recency at 0.5 and engagement at 0.3, a very recent post with moderate likes can beat an older viral post. Tune by measuring downstream engagement metrics.

Misconceptions
  • More signals do not guarantee better ranking without proper normalization.
  • High engagement may be noisy; combine with trust signals to avoid manipulation.
Key Takeaway

Start with a clear weighted sum, normalize and cap, then iterate using experiments and monitoring.

keyIdea.title: Practical code
keyIdea.text: A small Python heuristic demonstrates how recency, log-transformed likes and relationship strength combine into an interpretable ranking.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.4 › Ranking Heuristic — Code
Code (example)
import datetime
import math

def rank_posts(posts, current_user_id, user_interactions):
  ranked_posts = []
  now = datetime.datetime.now(datetime.timezone.utc)

  for post in posts:
    score = 0.0

    # Recency: decay over 24 * 7 hours (one week)
    time_diff = now - post['created_at']
    hours_since_post = time_diff.total_seconds() / 3600
    recency_score = max(0, 1 - (hours_since_post / (24 * 7)))
    score += 0.5 * recency_score

    # Engagement: log transform of likes and comments
    likes = post.get('likes_count', 0)
    comments = post.get('comments_count', 0)
    engagement_score = (math.log(likes + 1) * 0.1) + (comments * 0.5)
    score += 0.3 * min(100, engagement_score)

    # Relationship: interaction score capped to 1.0
    author_id = post['author_id']
    relationship_strength = user_interactions.get((current_user_id, author_id), 0)
    score += 0.2 * min(1.0, relationship_strength / 10.0)

    post['rank_score'] = score
    ranked_posts.append(post)

  ranked_posts.sort(key=lambda p: p['rank_score'], reverse=True)
  return ranked_posts
Explanation & tips
  • Use timezone-aware datetimes to compute recency correctly.
  • Log-transform likes to dampen extremes and cap engagement contributions.
  • Tune weights (0.5, 0.3, 0.2 here) with A/B tests and monitoring.
  • Simulate cold-start by zeroing relationship scores and show popular content.
Try this

Run the function with different weights and observe how the ranked order changes; log downstream metrics to validate improvements.

screens.title: ML for Ranking — From heuristics to learned models
screens.narratorSegment: Machine learning can replace fixed weights with models that predict engagement probability or a ranking score directly from features. Inputs typically include user history, post metadata, content embeddings, engagement signals and relationship features. The learned model outputs a score or ranking signal that the Feed Service uses to order candidates. The main advantage is that models can capture complex interactions among features and adapt as user behavior changes. But they also add operational complexity: models need training pipelines, feature stores, real-time feature computation, and offline evaluation. A common misconception is that ML always outperforms heuristics; in early stages simple heuristics with proper monitoring can be faster to iterate and safer. When adopting ML, run shadow experiments and A/B tests, and cache model inferences for common segments to reduce latency. Also monitor for feedback loops where the model amplifies narrow content; inject diversity constraints or secondary objectives when needed. Concrete example: a classifier predicts click probability which is multiplied by recency decay for final ranking. What features would you include in the model for your product? keyIdea.text: ML models can learn complex signal interactions but require feature pipelines, training and careful evaluation; heuristics remain useful early on.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.4 › Machine Learning
Typical features
  • User history and past engagement signals.
  • Post metadata and content embeddings.
  • Author signals, time features and device/context signals.
Operational needs
  • Feature store and consistent online features.
  • Training pipeline, offline evaluation and model validation.
  • Latency budgets and caching of model inferences.
Key Takeaway

Use ML when signal complexity justifies operational cost; always validate via controlled experiments and monitor for echo chamber effects.

screens.title: Real-time Updates and Freshness
screens.narratorSegment: Freshness is a core user expectation: new posts should surface quickly. For push-based feeds freshness is inherent since posts are fanned out at write time. For pull or hybrid systems you need strategies to reduce the delay between a post being created and a user seeing it. Caching ranked feed segments is common, but caches must be invalidated or incrementally updated when new posts arrive. Notifications via WebSockets or long-polling can inform clients there is new content without redoing full ranking. Background jobs or micro-batches can precompute top segments periodically to provide near-real-time responses while keeping compute bounded. A common mistake is assuming cached ranked segments don't need fine-grained invalidation; stale caches harm perceived freshness. Another important consideration is prioritization: high-visibility authors or posts might trigger immediate partial recomputation. Measure freshness with observable metrics like time-to-first-appearance and consider user expectations — for some apps a few seconds matter, in others minutes are acceptable. How would you trade off C P U cost to reduce time-to-first-appearance by ten seconds? Real-time Updates and Freshness means use push, notifications, incremental cache updates or background precomputation to keep feeds fresh while controlling compute costs.. In practical terms, making sure new posts appear quickly. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. narration.text: Freshness is a core user expectation: new posts should surface quickly. For push-based feeds freshness is inherent since posts are fanned out at write time. screens.title: Cold Start and Avoiding Filter Bubbles
screens.narratorSegment: Two social design problems often considered together are cold start and filter bubbles. Cold start occurs when a new user has little or no interaction history. A practical solution is to seed the feed with popular posts, suggested accounts, or category-based content until personal signals emerge. This gives new users a reasonable initial experience without waiting for full personalization. Filter bubbles arise when personalization narrows content to the point where users only see views that reinforce existing beliefs. To mitigate this, introduce diversity or serendipity: down-weight repeated authors or topics, inject topical exploration items, or introduce a small randomization factor. A misconception is to treat diversity as purely aesthetic; it actually protects long-term engagement and healthy discovery. When testing these strategies, compare short-term engagement lifts to long-term retention metrics. For example, giving a new user a mix of popular and exploratory posts may reduce immediate clicks but increase retention over weeks. Ask: how will you measure discovery versus immediate engagement in your product? screens.title: Reducing Compute: Caching and Precomputation
screens.narratorSegment: Computational cost is a central production concern. Ranking thousands of posts for millions of users in real time is expensive. Common mitigations include caching ranked segments per user or cohort, precomputing heavy model inferences offline then serving cached scores, and using incremental updates instead of full recomputation. Cache expiration should balance freshness with cost: short TTLs keep content fresher but increase recompute. Another approach is to compute only a small top window eagerly and compute deeper pages lazily. Use aggressive caching for cold or inactive users where updates are rare. Specialized hardware, such as GPUs, may be justified for large-scale model inference but often the first optimizations are software-level: serve cached ranked slices, cache per-author recent posts, and reuse feature computations. A typical misconception is to over-optimize for latency without measuring whether the user experience improves. Instrument requests, cache hits and compute time; use those signals to pick the most cost-effective optimizations. What cache TTL would you choose if your product values immediacy highly? Module 11 › Chapter 11.4 › Performance & Caching
Cache patterns
  • Per-user ranked slice caching (top N items).
  • Per-author recent posts caching for fast pulls.
  • Feature caches for expensive model inputs.
Incremental updates

Update only affected cached slices when a new post from an author arrives instead of recomputing all users' feeds. This reduces write and compute amplification.

Key Takeaway

Measure compute cost and cache hit rates first. Apply cached slices, incremental updates and feature caching before investing in specialized hardware.

screens.title: A/B Testing, Metrics and Common Mistakes
screens.narratorSegment: Ranking changes must be evaluated through controlled experiments. A/B testing lets you compare new heuristics or models against production by measuring key metrics: click-through rate, time spent, downstream retention and negative signals like hides or reports. Always run experiments with sufficient duration and sample size to capture longer-term effects. Common mistakes include optimizing short-term clicks at the expense of retention, ignoring negative engagement signals, or failing to segment experiments by device or user cohort. Another frequent error is not instrumenting enough telemetry — log ordering, rank positions, and exposures so you can diagnose why a change behaved a certain way. When you detect regressions, roll back incrementally and investigate feature drift or data quality issues. Finally, document and automate rollout policies so good experiments can graduate to production reliably. Think about what metric you would prioritize for your product: immediate engagement or sustained retention? fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we'll follow how raw posts become a personalized news feed. You'll learn the two common aggregation patterns — push and pull — why merging many sources can become a bottleneck, and how ranking transforms thousands of candidate posts into a compact, relevant set. We'll examine the signals used by modern ranking: recency, engagement, relationship strength, content type and author authority. I will show a simple scoring formula and a hands-on Python heuristic you can implement. We will also cover operational concerns: keeping feeds fresh in real time, handling new users with no history, preventing filter bubbles, and avoiding expensive per-request computation through caching and efficient merging. By the end you'll be able to reason about which parts of feed generation to push down into pre-computation, which signals to treat as fast features, and when to use machine learning models to replace heuristics. Think of this chapter as the roadmap that connects storage and fanout choices to the user-facing ordering that drives engagement. How would you balance recency and engagement for your product? That question will guide much of our examples.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to describe the two primary aggregation patterns for feeds and explain when each is appropriate. You will understand how merging many sorted post lists can become a computational bottleneck and why heap-based merging reduces memory and time costs. You will name the principal signals used to rank posts — recency, engagement, relationship strength, content type and author credibility — and you will be able to write a simple weighted scoring function combining these signals. Finally, you'll be able to discuss production concerns: real-time freshness strategies, the cold-start problem for new users, the risk of filter bubbles, and practical mitigations like caching and A/B testing. Each objective combines definition with practice: you will see concrete examples and a small Python heuristic to implement and test locally. These competencies prepare you to design feed subsystems that balance latency, accuracy, and compute cost.

These objectives emphasize practical judgement. You will practice writing a scoring function and running small experiments to see how weights change ordering. I will show when a push-based precomputation improves latency and when a pull or hybrid approach keeps storage costs lower. We'll walk through an example where a user follows a thousand accounts, and you'll see how naive retrieval creates large candidate sets that must be merged and scored efficiently. We'll also explore the cold-start strategy of showing popular or suggested content until personalization signals arrive, and why diversity should sometimes be injected deliberately to avoid filter bubbles. Finally, you will learn which metrics to use in A/B tests — click-through, time spent and retention — and how those choices shape ranking trade-offs. These skills prepare you to propose concrete system-level changes rather than just conceptual ideas.

Aggregation is the stage where candidate posts are gathered before ranking. In a push-based system, when an author publishes a post the system fans out that post to the followers' inboxes — those per-user stores already contain the candidates, so a feed request simply reads a small pre-ordered list. This minimizes read-time latency but increases write amplification and storage. In a pull-based system the feed service identifies whom the user follows and fetches recent posts from each followed account when the user requests a feed. Pull reduces write cost and storage, but it can produce large candidate sets and higher read latency. A hybrid approach precomputes popular authors' posts while pulling for less active accounts, balancing cost and latency. Consider a user who follows a thousand accounts: a pure pull that fetches ten posts per account creates ten thousand candidates; that is the classic merging problem. The practical rule is to push when reads vastly outnumber writes and storage is acceptable, pull when writes dominate or storage is constrained, and hybrid when neither extreme fits. A misconception is to assume push is always better — it can cause excessive storage and updating for high-write users. Question: given your product's read/write profile, which strategy will likely give better user-perceived latency?

When a pull or hybrid strategy yields many candidate lists, naive concatenation and sorting is expensive. An efficient approach uses a heap to merge sorted lists and keep only the top-K results. The idea is simple: treat the latest post from each followed user's list as an entry, insert those entries into a min-heap or max-heap sized to K, and then repeatedly pull the next most recent item from the list that produced the popped heap element. This way you never materialize all candidates at once. For example, if you want the top 50 posts from 1,000 followees, you initialize the heap with the newest post from each followee and only fetch the next post from a followee when its head was part of the top-K candidate set. This reduces memory and network reads. Common misconceptions include assuming heaps eliminate all work — they reduce memory and sorting costs but you still need to fetch posts and metadata. Another important point: pick the right heap orientation (min vs max) and choose K that matches the UI (page size plus a small buffer). Practical tip: combine heap merging with caching of recent per-user post lists so the fetchs used by the heap are low-latency. How could you instrument your system to measure savings from heap-based merging?

Ranking is where the candidate list becomes the user's actual feed. Ranking factors are the measurable features that indicate a post's likely value to a user. Recency remains an important baseline: newer posts are often more relevant. Engagement — likes, comments, shares and views — signals popularity and often correlates with user interest. Relationship strength captures how closely a user interacts with an author, and content type lets you prefer media formats users like. Author authority or credibility acts as a tie-breaker for expert content. Finally, diversity is a design signal used to prevent a feed from being dominated by one source or topic. A simple misconception is treating engagement as absolute truth; high engagement can be misleading due to bots or viral noise, which is why signals are combined and sometimes capped. Another common mistake is over-weighting explicit user preferences, which can create a filter bubble. In practice, a scoring function sums weighted signals and then sorts posts by score. You can test different weight combinations with small experiments to see how ordering and engagement change. Ask yourself: which signal would you reduce to increase serendipity in the feed?

A scoring function turns multiple signals into a single numeric priority. A simple form is a weighted sum: Score = W1 * Recency + W2 * Engagement + W3 * Relationship + …. This makes reasoning straightforward: increase a weight to favor a signal, decrease it to reduce influence. The chapter provides a small Python example where recency decays over seven days, engagement aggregates likes and comments with different weights, and relationship strength is an external feature. In practice, you should cap extreme values, normalize different signals, and consider transforms like logarithms for counts. A common misconception is to assume more signals always improve quality — noisy or correlated signals can add instability. Another is to place absolute trust in the initial weights; A/B testing and logging are essential to validate that your weight choices lift metrics. Concrete example: weight recency at 0.5, engagement at 0.3 and relationship at 0.2 and observe how a very recent low-engagement post might outrank an older high-engagement post. The final question is: what tradeoff do you accept between freshness and popularity for your feed?

Let's walk through a hands-on Python ranking heuristic that follows the chapter template. The code calculates a recency score using a simple decay, a likes-based engagement score with a logarithmic transform, and a relationship bonus capped at one. After computing the score for each post, the function sorts posts by score and returns the ordered list. This example is intentionally simple so you can experiment with weights and transforms. A common pitfall is forgetting timezone-aware timestamps; always use timezone-aware datetimes for correct recency. Another mistake is not limiting extreme counts — use math transforms or caps. Use this code locally: change weights to see how results reorder, or simulate new users by clearing relationship scores to observe cold-start behavior. When you run experiments, log both ordering and downstream engagement to validate whether score changes improve real metrics. Which weight would you change first to make the feed show more recent content?
